authors: Minkova, Kristina and Chakravarthy, Shashank M. and van Dijck, Gijs
title: Low-Resource Deontic Modality Classification in EU Legislation
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the Natural Legal Language Processing Workshop 2023 (ACL Anthology), pp. 149-158
what_it_says: Labels 200 sampled EU regulation provisions with six deontic classes (obligation, permission, power, prohibition, right, none) by three annotators. A small non pretrained fusion model beat fine tuned Legal-BERT on macro F1 (about 0.61 against 0.45), obligations dominate the data, and rare classes were not recognised.
why_relevant: Closest prior task to our binding status coding: clause level force labels on legislation with a small human annotated set and per annotator labels. We would cite it for the class imbalance point (report agreement and macro scores beside accuracy). It differs: it labels the modality of a sentence inside one legal family, while we code the force of a whole provision in guidance, standards and law, with a testing focus.

authors: O'Neill, James and Buitelaar, Paul and Robin, Cecile and O'Brien, Leona
title: Classifying sentential modality in legal language: a use case in financial regulations, acts and directives
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the 16th International Conference on Artificial Intelligence and Law (ICAIL 2017)
what_it_says: Classifies sentences of financial regulation as obligation, prohibition or permission using ensembles of neural networks over legal and general embeddings, and uses calibrated probabilities as a proxy for degree of obligation. Best accuracy reported is 82.33 percent on held out data.
why_relevant: Early example of modality classification in regulation that motivates why a modal verb rule is a natural baseline. We cite it in the baselines section. It differs: three classes, finance domain, no category for non binding recommendation or for ambiguous force. Only the abstract page was read.

authors: Guldimann, Philipp and Spiridonov, Alexander and Staab, Robin and Jovanovic, Nikola and Vero, Mark and Vechev, Velko and Gueorguieva, Anna-Maria and Balunovic, Mislav and Konstantinov, Nikola and Bielik, Pavol and Tsankov, Petar and Vechev, Martin
title: COMPL-AI Framework: A Technical Interpretation and LLM Benchmarking Suite for the EU Artificial Intelligence Act
what_it_says: Translates EU AI Act requirements into technical requirements tagged by system category and links each to existing benchmarks, then evaluates 12 language models. Some requirements (for example explainability, corrigibility) lack usable technical definitions, and the authors state the results are not legally binding.
why_relevant: Shows that mapping the Act to concrete tests is an active effort and that the Act leaves metrics open, which supports our reading that binding text seldom says how to test. We would cite it in related work and the discussion of what a provision requires. It differs: it operationalises the Act for one model type, while we record what documents say across families and how binding each statement is.

authors: METR (authors not named in the document)
title: Common Elements of Frontier AI Safety Policies
venue_or_publisher: METR report (March 2025 update; first version August 2024)
what_it_says: Compares twelve company frontier safety policies and finds nine shared components, among them capability thresholds, evaluation timing and frequency, full capability elicitation and conditions for halting deployment. The policies are voluntary and the report counts presence of components without testing whether they are followed. The text read was cut off part way through.
why_relevant: Direct cross document comparison of what evaluation commitments exist, which we cite as the nearest comparison for the voluntary company layer. It is grey literature, so we would mark it as such. It differs: company commitments only, presence or absence coding, no force coding and no government documents. Reading was partial because the fetched text was truncated.

authors: Arnold, Zachary and Schiff, Daniel S. and Schiff, Kaylyn Jackson and Love, Brian and Melot, Jennifer and Singh, Neha and Jenkins, Lindsay and Lin, Ashley and Pilz, Konstantin and Enweareazu, Ogadinma and Girard, Tyler
title: Introducing the AI Governance and Regulatory Archive (AGORA): An Analytic Infrastructure for Navigating the Emerging AI Governance Landscape
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2024), vol. 7, pp. 39-48
what_it_says: Presents a curated and annotated dataset of AI laws and policies with a taxonomy of risks, harms, governance strategies, incentives and application domains (over 330 instruments at launch). The dataset documentation (also read) says documents are split into segments, tagged with a 77 code codebook and validated by a second annotator, with US federal coverage heaviest.
why_relevant: Most relevant existing segment level annotation of AI governance texts, so reviewers will ask how our table differs. We would cite it as the nearest dataset and as a source for locating documents. It differs: AGORA tags topics and strategies, not binding force or test type, and does not report row level verification against the source. Abstract page and dataset documentation were read, not the full paper.

authors: Brandsma, Gijs Jan and Blom-Hansen, Jens and Meijer, Christiaan and Moodley, Kody
title: Computational Identification of Regulatory Statements in EU Legislation
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (publication venue not stated in the text read)
what_it_says: Classifies sentences containing shall or must in about 120,000 EU legal acts as regulatory or not, using the ADICO institutional grammar, with 7,200 hand labelled sentences. A dependency parse rule approach reached about 0.80 accuracy and a Legal-BERT plus XGBoost model about 0.84, and the two disagreed often.
why_relevant: Supports a rule against learned model comparison on legal text and the caution that modal words alone do not settle whether a sentence regulates. We would cite it beside our wording rule baseline. It differs: it separates regulatory from non regulatory statements within binding EU law, while we grade force across binding and non binding documents.

authors: Hassani, Shabnam and Sabetzadeh, Mehrdad and Amyot, Daniel
title: An Empirical Study on LLM-based Classification of Requirements-related Provisions in Food-safety Regulations
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated in the text read)
what_it_says: Classifies regulatory provisions by the requirements concepts they contain, comparing fine tuned BERT and GPT models, few shot GPT-4o, and simpler baselines (BiLSTM, keyword lookup). Fine tuned models beat the baselines, few shot raised recall but lowered precision, and generalisation to US provisions rests on only 50 sentences. The last part of the paper was not read.
why_relevant: Requirements engineering precedent for comparing language model classification of provisions with simple baselines and for reporting annotator agreement (kappa about 0.90 on one label). We would cite it for the baseline design. It differs: topic content labels in one domain, not binding force.

authors: Sleimi, Amin and Sannier, Nicolas and Sabetzadeh, Mehrdad and Briand, Lionel and Ceci, Marcello and Dann, John
title: An Automated Framework for the Extraction of Semantic Legal Metadata from Legal Texts
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (extends a Requirements Engineering 2018 conference paper; journal not verified)
what_it_says: Rule based extraction over parse trees of modality (obligation, permission, prohibition), conditions and many other legal metadata types, tested on Luxembourgish traffic and other codes. Reported phrase level precision was about 97 percent and recall about 95 percent in one domain, and precision fell to about 82 percent in another. The final quarter of the text was not read.
why_relevant: Shows that marker lists for modality and conditions are an established method in requirements engineering, which supports our wording rule baseline and our conditional class (trigger words). It differs: French national statutes, modality limited to three values, no non binding category.

authors: Stelling, Lily and Murray, Malcolm and Galizzi, Bruno and Schaffelder, Max and Campos, Simeon and Papadatos, Henry
title: Evaluating AI Providers' Frontier AI Safety Frameworks
what_it_says: Scores twelve company frontier safety frameworks against 65 weighted criteria and finds scores from 8 to 34 percent. It notes that discretionary wording such as may consider is common for important actions and that frameworks work better as internal tools than external accountability. The last part of the text was not read.
why_relevant: Evidence that wording strength in safety documents is itself an object of study, supporting our focus on force. We cite it in related work. It differs: company voluntary frameworks, scored against a risk management ideal, not coded by force and test type across government documents.

authors: Campos, Simeon and Papadatos, Henry and Roger, Fabien and Touzet, Chloe and Quarks, Otter and Murray, Malcolm
title: A Frontier AI Risk Management Framework: Bridging the Gap Between Current AI Practices and Established Risk Management
what_it_says: Conceptual framework adapting risk management from aviation and nuclear sectors (risk identification, analysis, treatment, governance) to frontier AI, relating company frameworks to standards such as ISO/IEC 23894 and the NIST framework. It is not empirically validated and argues no regulator yet sets AI risk tolerance.
why_relevant: Background for where pre deployment testing sits within risk management, to cite when explaining why testing appears under assurance and treatment in standards. It differs: normative proposal, not a table of what documents state.

authors: Marino, Bill and Hunter, Rosco and Schnabl, Christoph and Jamali, Zubair and Kalpakos, Marinos E. and Kashyap, Mudra and Hinton, Isaiah and Hanson, Alexa and Nazir, Maahum and Steffek, Felix and Wen, Hongkai and Lane, Nicholas
title: AIReg-Bench: Benchmarking Language Models That Assess AI Regulation Compliance
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint; also listed as a NeurIPS 2026 AI4GOOD workshop poster
what_it_says: Benchmark of 120 synthetic technical documentation excerpts, each rated by three legal experts for compliance with an AI Act article (Krippendorff alpha 0.651), on which ten language models are compared with the expert median. The best model reached quadratic kappa 0.863 and several models were more lenient than humans. Only the final few thousand characters were not read.
why_relevant: Most direct evidence on language models judging AI Act text with expert labels and moderate human agreement, which we cite in the coder agreement study discussion to justify reporting agreement between model coders and against the original coding. It differs: it judges system documentation against articles, we code the force of the regulatory text itself.

authors: Stelling, Lily and Yang, Mick and Gipiskis, Rokas and Staufer, Leon and Chin, Ze Shen and Campos, Simeon and Gil, Ariel and Chen, Michael
title: Mapping Industry Practices to the EU AI Act's GPAI Code of Practice Safety and Security Measures
what_it_says: Maps the safety and security commitments of the third draft of the Code of Practice for general purpose AI to quotes from company documents and finds that most measures have support from at least three companies, with gaps in areas such as external assessors and incident reporting. It does not assess compliance and uses a draft since revised.
why_relevant: Comparable quote based mapping from regulatory text to evidence, and a reminder that the Code is a voluntary route to the Act. We would cite it when discussing general purpose model testing. It differs: maps company practice to one draft code, not binding force across many regulators.

title: Decoding Global AI Governance: A Computational Linguistic Analysis of National Regulations
venue_or_publisher: Proceedings of the AAAI/ACM Conference on AI, Ethics, and Society (AIES 2024), student abstract
what_it_says: Analyses 1,065 AI strategy and legislation documents from 64 countries with text embeddings and a hedging measure, and reports that hard laws score higher on tentativeness than soft laws and that many documents resemble the EU texts. It is a short abstract with limited method detail.
why_relevant: A document level text analysis of hedging language across AI governance documents, so it is the nearest use of language cues for force. We would cite it and note it is a student abstract with an undefined measure. It differs: whole document similarity, not clause level coding.

authors: Ariai, Farid and Mackenzie, Joel and Demartini, Gianluca
title: Natural Language Processing for the Legal Domain: A Survey of Tasks, Datasets, Models and Challenges
venue_or_publisher: arXiv preprint (venue not stated in the text read)
what_it_says: PRISMA based survey of 131 studies on legal NLP tasks, datasets and models, listing classification tasks such as deontic modality tagging in contracts and unfair clause detection. It notes datasets concentrate in EU, US, Chinese and Swiss jurisdictions. The last part of the text was not read.
why_relevant: Gives reviewers a general survey to anchor the claim that legal text classification is established while AI governance text is not covered. We would cite it once in related work. It differs: broad survey with no AI governance corpus.

authors: Ferraro, Gabriela and Lam, Ho Pun
title: NLP techniques for normative mining
venue_or_publisher: IfCoLoG Journal of Logics and their Applications, vol. 8(4), pp. 941-974
what_it_says: Reviews challenges of extracting legal norms from text and surveys semantic parsing techniques for turning legal text into machine interpretable norms.
why_relevant: Peer reviewed overview of extracting norms from legal text, for one sentence in related work on normative mining. It differs: methods overview, no AI governance data. Only the abstract page was read.

authors: Davvetas, Athanasios and Papademas, Michael and Ziouvelou, Xenia and Karkaletsis, Vangelis
title: AI Act Evaluation Benchmark: An Open, Transparent, and Reproducible Evaluation Dataset for NLP and RAG Systems
what_it_says: Releases 339 language model generated scenarios linked to AI Act articles and obligation points, with risk level, article retrieval and obligation generation tasks. Labels come from model output under written rules and no expert validation or agreement is reported.
why_relevant: Another AI Act dataset to cite as unvalidated, to contrast with our rows that carry a verification status and a measured error rate. It differs: synthetic scenarios, not the text of provisions.

authors: Guliani, Keerat and Gill, Deepkamal and Landsman, David and Eshraghi, Nima and Kumar, Krishna and Gondara, Lovedeep
title: De Jure: Iterative LLM Self-Refinement for Structured Extraction of Regulatory Rules
what_it_says: Pipeline that turns sections of regulations (SEC, EU AI Act, HIPAA) into structured rules with a language model and language model judges that trigger regeneration. Quality is judged by models without reported agreement with human experts, and conditions and exceptions are the weakest part.
why_relevant: Representative of automatic extraction of rules from the AI Act, which we cite to say model extraction is possible but its checking is model based. It differs: no human check, no force classes; our design pairs model coding with blind second codings and a source check.

title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels (RFC 2119, BCP 14)
what_it_says: Defines MUST as an absolute requirement, SHOULD as allowing valid reasons to ignore in particular circumstances, and MAY as truly optional, for use in IETF standards track documents.
why_relevant: Source for a formal definition of requirement levels behind a modal verb wording rule, and an example that conventions for shall, should and may differ between document families (this convention is not stated to apply to law). Not a scholarly article; page read in full, it is short.
